meta.subtitle: GAAP profit has arrived and cash generation is real, but volume is outrunning revenue and one customer still sets the terms

analystSentiment.commentary: We rate Marqeta HOLD with a $15 to $21 target range built around a Base case of $18. The 10-Q for the quarter ended June 30, 2026 shows a business that is growing and has turned profitable on a GAAP basis: Q2'26 revenue of $176M rose 17% year on year and the operating margin was 2.1%. Three things keep us from buying. Processing volume is growing faster than revenue, and the 10-Q MD&A explains part of the mechanism: Revenue Share rates paid to customers rise as their volumes rise. The 10-K risk factors name Block among a small number of customers that generate significant net revenue, so a single renewal can reset the model. And the vendor share count does not reconcile with the class totals in the April 2026 proxy, which makes per-share multiples less certain than usual. Against that, FY25 free cash flow of $160.8M and a TTM FCF yield of 11.5% give the shares support that the 183.9x trailing P/E hides. We would turn more constructive on evidence that revenue growth is holding up as volume scales, or on a Block renewal that does not cut pricing.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: Marqeta, Inc. runs a cloud-based open API platform for card issuing and transaction processing, headquartered in Oakland, California and incorporated in 2010. Per the 10-Q MD&A, every customer takes issuer processor services as the core offering; customers can add Bank and Network Management, Program Management (chargebacks, dispute resolution, reconciliation, card fulfillment) and Value Added Services such as tokenization and real-time decisioning and fraud management. Revenue is mostly platform services revenue, net: Interchange Fees and processing fees, less Revenue Share paid back to customers. The company reports a single reportable segment. Verticals named in the company description include financial services, on-demand services, lending, expense management, e-commerce enablement and buy now, pay later providers.

thesis.label: HOLD
thesis.body: Marqeta has crossed into GAAP profitability while still growing revenue in the high teens, and it converts revenue to free cash at a high rate. The stock already reflects much of that: the shares trade near the low end of the 52-week range, yet the Street is mostly at Hold and the price discounts a steady path rather than a collapse. Our view is that upside to the Street consensus target of $20.50 needs revenue to keep pace with volume, and the 10-Q MD&A gives a structural reason it may not. With customer concentration unresolved and a share-count question open, we think the risk and reward are roughly balanced at $16.55.

catalysts: Further quarters of GAAP net income would confirm that the Q2 2026 profit is a run-rate rather than a one-off; the Financials section sets out the quarter.
Evidence that revenue growth holds near the TTM pace as FY26E consensus revenue of ~$704M is tested; the Growth section covers the gap between volume and revenue.
A Block renewal on terms that do not reduce pricing would remove the overhang the Risks section describes.
Continued repurchases funded from free cash flow, discussed under Capital allocation.
risks: Customer concentration: the 10-K risk factors name Block among a few significant customers and flag renewals on less favorable terms.
Take-rate compression as Revenue Share rates step up with customer volume, per the 10-Q MD&A.
Liquidity buffer has thinned after heavy buybacks; the Balance sheet commentary covers the trend.
Dual class voting concentration limits what outside holders can influence; see Governance.

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.incomeCommentary: Q2'26 was the quarter the income statement turned. The 10-Q MD&A reports net income of $7,567 thousand for the three months ended June 30, 2026, after a small net loss in the same quarter of 2025. Net revenue rose to $175,995 thousand from $150,392 thousand. Gross margin held at 69% in both Q2 periods, so the improvement came from below gross profit: total operating expenses rose to $118,237 thousand from $113,289 thousand, much slower than revenue. Adjusted EBITDA margin, a non-GAAP measure, moved to 21% from 19%. The trailing picture is weaker than the quarter, with a TTM operating margin of -1.9% and FY25 operating margin of -7.4%, so one profitable quarter does not yet make a profitable year. The annual series also needs care: gross margin stepped from 48.7% in FY23 to 69.4% in FY24, which the 10-K risk factors tie to the August 2023 Block Amendment moving Card Network and Issuing Bank fees for the Cash App program into a reduction of net revenue. That presentation change, not an efficiency gain, explains the FY24 revenue decline of -25.0% and the margin step. Our read: the earnings trend is genuinely improving, but it rests on operating expense discipline that has to persist as the company invests.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.balanceCommentary: The balance sheet carries no reported debt, and cash and short-term investments of $0.7B at FY25 still cover a large share of the ~$1.7B market cap. The trend is the concern. Cash and short-term investments have fallen each year from $1.2B in FY21 and FY22, total equity has fallen from $1.6B in FY21 to $0.8B in FY25, and the current ratio dropped to 1.65 in FY25 from 3.37 a year earlier. The facts do not break out what sits in current liabilities, so we cannot say how much of the decline reflects settlement balances rather than lost cushion. The cause of the cash and equity decline is visible in the cash flow statement: repurchases, discussed below. The balance sheet remains sound, but it is no longer the excess-capital story it was, and further buybacks at the FY25 pace would need to come from free cash flow rather than the cash pile.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.cashflowCommentary: Free cash flow is the strongest part of the case. FY25 free cash flow was $160.8M, an FCF margin of 25.7%, up from 11.0% in FY24, and capital expenditure is small. Operating cash flow and free cash flow are nearly identical across the five years, which fits an asset-light processor. The counterweight is how the cash was used: FY25 share repurchases were well above free cash flow, which is why cash fell even in a strong cash year. The FCF margin also runs well ahead of the GAAP operating margin, and the facts do not include a bridge, so we treat part of the FY25 cash strength as working-capital timing until a second year confirms it. Our view is that cash generation is real and supports the valuation floor, but the FY25 margin is not a safe base to extrapolate.

multiples.note: Peer multiples pending a peer data source.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: On earnings the stock looks expensive and on cash it looks cheap, and the gap between the two is the valuation debate. Trailing P/E is 183.9x and EV/EBITDA is 62.9x because GAAP earnings are barely positive. Forward P/E falls to 61.3x on the NTM view and ~33.1x on FY27E consensus EPS of $0.50, with FY26E EPS at $0.27; the vendor does not state whether these consensus figures are GAAP or adjusted, so we do not treat the forward multiples as GAAP-based. P/S is 2.5x and the TTM FCF yield is 11.5%. One caveat applies to every per-share and market-cap figure: the Quote derives ~104.1M shares from the ~$1.7B market cap, while the proxy reports 392,067,528 Class A and 32,808,210 Class B shares outstanding as of April 15, 2026. The sources do not explain the difference, and we have used the vendor market cap and multiples as given. The Street is cautious too, with 14 analysts at 3 Buy, 10 Hold and 1 Sell and targets from $17.00 to $28.00 around a median of $19.50. We think the cash yield argues against a large downside from here, while the earnings multiple argues against paying up before profits compound.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Revenue growth stays close to the Q2'26 pace and operating expense discipline continues, so GAAP profit compounds into FY27E consensus EPS of $0.50 and above. Both conditions have to hold together. The shares rerate toward the Street consensus target of $20.50 and beyond, still inside the $17.00 to $28.00 target range.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Revenue lands near FY26E consensus of ~$704M with growth slowing toward the +13% the Street expects, GAAP profit stays thin, and the stock settles between the low end of the Street target range and the median of $19.50.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Either Block renews on less favorable terms, or Revenue Share step-ups widen the gap between volume and revenue enough to stall growth. Either route alone pushes the operating margin back below zero and takes the shares below the 52-week low of $14.80.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: We weight Bear above Bull because the two cases differ in shape. Bull needs two things at once: sustained revenue growth and continued cost discipline. Bear needs either one of two independent events, a weaker Block renewal or take-rate erosion, and both are named in the company's own filings. The Base case carries the most weight because the Q2'26 results support the consensus revenue path for FY26 without yet proving the earnings path for FY27. The probability-weighted value sits modestly above the current price, which is consistent with a HOLD rather than a BUY. The FCF yield is the reason we do not set Bear lower: a business converting revenue to cash at the FY25 rate should find buyers well before the price reflects a structural decline.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: Marqeta reports a single reportable segment, so all FY25 revenue of $624.9M sits in one line and no product or geographic split is available. Within it, the 10-Q MD&A describes two revenue components: platform services revenue, net, which carries Interchange Fees net of Revenue Share plus processing and other fees, and other services revenue, mainly card fulfillment. The economics turn on the platform line, where pricing to customers and incentives from Card Networks both move with volume. TPV for FY25 was $382.5 billion per the 10-K risk factors.

moatFactors.name: Embedded infrastructure and switching costs
moatFactors.body: Per the 10-Q MD&A, customers embed Marqeta to avoid building complex compliance elements and customer support services themselves, and the company manages Issuing Bank relationships and Card Network rule compliance for them. That makes a working card program costly to move. The counter-case is that large customers can negotiate hard at renewal, which the Block Amendment shows.

moatFactors.name: Volume-based network incentives
moatFactors.body: The 10-Q MD&A says Card Network incentives reach a higher cumulative rate as processing volumes increase, which rewards scale in costs of revenue. The same section says Revenue Share rates paid to customers also rise with volume, so part of the scale benefit is passed through rather than kept.

moatFactors.name: Customer concentration
moatFactors.body: The 10-K risk factors state the company generates significant net revenue from a small number of customers, including Block. A moat that depends on one relationship is narrower than the platform description implies.

businessMoat.durability: We rate the moat NARROW. The switching costs are real, because customers outsource compliance, bank sponsorship and network management rather than run them in-house. But the pricing evidence cuts the other way: the Block Amendment reduced pricing for Cash App, and Revenue Share terms are built to give customers more as they grow. The 10-K risk factors also describe markets that are competitive and continuously evolving, without naming rivals. The advantage looks durable enough to retain customers, but not strong enough to hold price with the customers that matter most.

points: Volume growth is strong: the 10-Q MD&A reports Q2'26 TPV rising to $120,423 million from $91,386 million a year earlier, and the 10-K risk factors report FY25 TPV up 31%.

Revenue is growing more slowly than volume. Q2'26 revenue rose 17% while TPV grew considerably faster, and the 10-Q MD&A explains one reason: Revenue Share rates rise as customer volumes rise. The filing does not quantify how much of the gap that mechanism explains, and we do not assume it is the whole story.

Consensus expects deceleration: FY26E revenue of ~$704M implies +13% growth after FY25 revenue of $624.9M grew +23.3%, and FY27E revenue of $807.2M. We see the FY26 estimate as reachable given the six-month results in the 10-Q.

The 10-K risk factors list expansion outside the United States, new products and a more diversified customer base among the drivers of future revenue growth. None is quantified in the facts, so we give them no weight in the Base case.

The counter-case to growth is that FY25's rebound partly laps the presentation change from the August 2023 Block Amendment, which depressed FY24 revenue; underlying growth is better judged on the quarterly comparison in the 10-Q.

management.leadership: The proxy statement dated 2026-04-21 lists Mike Milotich, Patti Kangwangkij, Todd Pollak and Crystal Sumner among the named executive officers, and identifies Simon Khalaf as the former Chief Executive Officer. The excerpt does not give the current titles of the other officers, so we do not assign roles. The same proxy refers to a former Executive Chairman without naming the person in the excerpt. A recent change at the top is therefore evident, but the excerpt does not say why it happened or who now leads the company, and we cannot judge the new team on a record the sources do not provide. The Q2'26 cost discipline is the clearest evidence available on execution.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation has leaned heavily toward buybacks. FY25 share repurchases were well above FY25 free cash flow, and repurchases have grown each year since FY22 in the cash flow facts. The company pays no dividend. The 10-K risk factors caution that the share repurchase program may not enhance long-term stockholder value and may reduce working capital. Our view is that buying back shares near the bottom of the 52-week range is defensible when the FCF yield is 11.5%, but the FY25 pace drew down the cash buffer, and a pace closer to free cash flow would be the more prudent course while Block terms remain uncertain.
management.governance: Per the proxy statement dated 2026-04-21, the Board determined that eight directors are independent under Nasdaq standards: Mmes. Atkinson, Cummings, Paul and Thomas and Messrs. Chokshi, Graf, Linville and Prasad. Jud Linville has served as independent Board Chair since June 2024, and the proxy cites his past role as Chief Executive Officer of Global Cards and Consumer Services at Citigroup Inc. The structure that matters most is the dual class. The 10-K risk factors state that it concentrates voting control with Class B holders, including directors, executive officers and their affiliates, and that it may depress the Class A trading price. For outside Class A holders, an independent chair and committee structure provide oversight, but strategic outcomes such as a sale or a change in control are not theirs to decide.
management.insiderOwnership: As of April 15, 2026, per the proxy, Jason Gardner held 94.99% of Class B common stock and 46.92% of total voting power, and all directors and executive officers as a group held 48.62% of total voting power. The excerpt does not state Mr. Gardner's current role. The proxy also lists other 5% holders, including entities associated with T. Rowe Price Associates at 14.34% of Class A and 7.81% of voting power, and entities associated with BlackRock, Inc. at 7.20% of Class A; the Vanguard row is listed without figures in the excerpt. Insider voting control near half the total means one holder's view effectively decides contested votes, which aligns that holder with the long term but leaves Class A investors with little leverage.

idiosyncratic: Block concentration: the 10-K risk factors state that the company generates significant net revenue from a small number of customers, including Block, and that losing or renewing these relationships on less favorable terms could hurt results. The August 2023 Block Amendment already reduced pricing once, so this is a demonstrated risk rather than a hypothetical one. Watch for any renewal disclosure.

Take-rate compression: the 10-Q MD&A states that Revenue Share is recorded as a reduction to net revenue and that rates rise as customer volumes rise. If volume growth concentrates in large customers, revenue growth could keep lagging TPV. Watch the gap between TPV and revenue growth each quarter.

Share-count uncertainty: the vendor share count of ~104.1M does not reconcile with the Class A and Class B totals in the April 2026 proxy, and the sources do not explain why. Until it is resolved, every per-share multiple in this report carries more error than usual.

Bank and network dependence: the 10-K risk factors state that the company relies on relationships with Issuing Banks and Card Networks, and that losing them could hurt the business. Network incentives in costs of revenue also depend on hitting volume thresholds, per the 10-Q MD&A.
risks.systemic: The 10-Q MD&A states that management cannot predict how macroeconomic factors, including inflation, interest rates, geopolitical conflicts and uncertainty from potential tariffs, will affect processing volumes. Because revenue is tied to Interchange Fees and processing fees, a slowdown in consumer spending would flow through to revenue quickly. Regulation is a second channel: the 10-K risk factors note that rules applying directly and through Issuing Banks and Card Networks are subject to change and uncertain interpretation. Interest rates matter in a smaller way, because other income consists primarily of interest on short-term investments and cash deposits, and that income shrinks as cash is spent on buybacks or as rates fall. We see these risks as cyclical rather than thesis-breaking, but they would amplify a Bear case driven by Block or pricing.

body: HOLD, target range $15 to $21. Marqeta has shown it can grow revenue in the high teens, earn a GAAP profit and generate substantial free cash flow, and those qualities support the shares near the bottom of their 52-week range.

We stop short of BUY because volume growth is not fully reaching revenue, customer concentration with Block remains unresolved, and a share-count discrepancy between the vendor and the proxy leaves the per-share valuation less certain than it looks. We would revisit the rating on two more quarters of GAAP profit with revenue growth holding up, or on a Block renewal that preserves pricing.
